solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Unfair attempt to limit travel time on vacation

indicators.note: to limit something is to hem it in on both sides, so one piece encloses the others
a place on vacation is emptied, so the word keeps only its outer letters with the inside gone

blocks.note: a bid is an attempt, as in a bid for power
to go is to travel
the word with its middle letters cleared out

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a scheme to restrict how long holidaymakers may spend travelling is unjust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' reads as being on holiday, but it is the empty-word device: a word on vacation keeps only its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigoted person judges others with prejudice rather than fairly, so the adjective works as a looser synonym for unjust.

clue.text: Happen to note there’s a ringer going about!

indicators.note: to go about something is to travel round it, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: a bell is a thing that rings
fa is the fourth note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a bell-ringer is wandering about, as if the music were following them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringer' tempts you towards a lookalike or a cheat; here it is simply something that rings.
explanation.definitionFit: When misfortune befalls someone it happens to them; the verb is literary and takes a direct object.

clue.text: Fish, good variety of tuna, given to a huge glutton

indicators.note: a variety is a different version, so these letters appear in a different form

blocks.note: the gar is a long-snouted fish
G is the standard abbreviation for good
the four letters rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fish, especially a good sort of tuna, is served to someone with an enormous appetite.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a menu; each word is in fact a piece, and the answer is the name of a famously greedy giant.
explanation.definitionFit: Gargantua is the giant in Rabelais whose vast appetite gave English the adjective gargantuan, so his name stands for any huge eater.

clue.text: Bird heading away from its last animal sanctuary

indicators.note: going away from its final letter means the word loses that letter

blocks.note: a title is the heading at the top of a piece of writing
Noah's ark sheltered the animals from the flood

explanation.surface: A bird leaves its final refuge for animals and heads off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird heading' reads like a bird setting off; 'Bird' is the definition alone and 'heading' is a noun, a title, which drops its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: The titlark is an old name for the meadow pipit, a small brown songbird of open country.

clue.text: Take apart books in pitiful English

indicators.note: placing something in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: dismal means pitifully poor, as in a dismal performance
NT, the New Testament, is a set of books
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A critic tears apart some books written in poor English.
explanation.walkthrough: The New Testament is the crossword's usual stand-in for books, so 'books' becomes two letters rather than a library.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismantle a machine or structure is to take it to pieces, so the phrase is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Calendar gals stripped (one not in the buff)

indicators.note: something stripped has its outer layer removed, so only the inside letters survive
saying a thing is not in a word means it must be taken out

blocks.note: the word without its first and last letters
a buff is an enthusiast, and a maniac is an obsessive fan
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A pin-up calendar of undressed girls, with one of them, oddly, not naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripped' and 'in the buff' both play on nudity. Here a buff is a fan, MANIAC, which loses its I.
explanation.definitionFit: An almanac is an annual publication arranged by days of the year, so it is a calendar with extra information.

clue.text: Porter perhaps cross, meeting a smart home help

blocks.note: porter is a dark beer, an example of ale
X is the shape of a cross
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cross hotel porter meets a smartly dressed domestic helper.
explanation.walkthrough: Porter looks like a doorman and cross like angry; in fact porter is a dark beer and the cross is the letter X.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexa is Amazon's voice assistant, which controls lights and other gadgets in a smart home.

clue.text: Confuse A&E maybe, with obscure case of pinkeye

indicators.note: a case is the outside covering, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: misty means blurred and hard to make out
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Accident and emergency staff are puzzled by an unclear case of conjunctivitis.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E reads as the hospital emergency department, but it means the letters A and E, which a careless typist may confuse.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitting A where E was meant is a typing slip, and 'maybe' marks this as one example.

clue.text: Irish male eleven finally getting score draw?

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word, so only its last letter is used

blocks.note: the final letter
a score draw is a tied match with goals, such as one all, with I as one

explanation.surface: An Irish football team ends up with a draw in which both sides scored.
explanation.walkthrough: In British football a score draw is a tie in which goals were scored, as opposed to nil-nil; the question mark admits one all is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Niall is a traditional Irish boy's name, borne by the legendary high king Niall of the Nine Hostages.

clue.text: A contemptuous person roughly upended lover in play

indicators.note: turning something on its end in a down entry makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a disser is someone who disses, or shows contempt for, others
C stands for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A scornful person rudely knocks over a lover during a stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' reads as rudely but gives C, for circa; A plus DISSER plus C then all turn over together.
explanation.definitionFit: Cressida is the Trojan woman loved by Troilus in Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida, so she is a lover in a play.

clue.text: Fragments taken from street of a trailer

indicators.note: broken fragments can be pieced together in a new order

blocks.note: all three words taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: Clips cut from a road sequence are used in a film trailer.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder is 'street of a', so 'of' is in the letters too; 'trailer' at the end is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A film trailer gives viewers a foretaste, an early sample of what is coming.

clue.text: Sophisticated small drone close to plane

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is taken

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
UAV, unmanned aerial vehicle, is the technical term for a drone
the final letter

explanation.surface: An advanced miniature drone flies near an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' looks like 'near', but it means the end of 'plane'.
explanation.definitionFit: A suave person is smoothly charming and polished in manner, which is the social meaning of sophisticated.

clue.text: Sinister body regulating ads in the City

blocks.note: sinister is Latin for left, and LH is left hand
the Advertising Standards Authority regulates UK advertising

explanation.surface: A shadowy advertising watchdog operates in the City of London's financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The City' suggests London's financial centre; here City alone is the definition. The ASA is Britain's Advertising Standards Authority.
explanation.definitionFit: Lhasa is the capital of Tibet, once called the Forbidden City, so it is a city in the plain geographic sense.

clue.text: Plant that’s difficult gardener is going to put in fine soil, initially

indicators.note: putting one thing in another places it inside, so the second piece wraps the first
initially points to the start of the word, so only its first letter is taken

blocks.note: the nursery rhyme's 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary' is asked how her garden grows
the contracted form of will, as in she'll
A1 means first-rate, written as A and I
the first letter

explanation.surface: A tricky plant that the gardener plans to set in finely tilled earth.
explanation.walkthrough: The contrary gardener comes from the nursery rhyme 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary'; 'fine' is A1, first-rate, written with the letter I for the digit.
explanation.definitionFit: The amaryllis is a bulb grown for its large trumpet-shaped flowers, so it is one kind of plant.

clue.text: Retire due to ill health, maybe eventually like one’s teacher?

blocks.clueFragment: Retire due to ill health, maybe
blocks.note: first meaning: go to bed and stay there because one is unwell
second meaning: study for a BEd, the teaching degree, and so end up qualified like one's teacher

explanation.surface: Someone takes early retirement on medical grounds, perhaps following in their old teacher's footsteps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retire' suggests leaving work, but here it means going to bed. A BEd, Bachelor of Education, is the degree many British teachers hold.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes an invalid confined to bed, while the pun reads the last word as the teaching degree.

clue.text: Spouse exercising for health

indicators.note: exercising works something hard, so these letters are worked into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: A husband or wife working out to stay fit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one partner going to the gym; 'exercising' is the signal and the two words after it are the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: One's other half is a jokey idiom for one's husband, wife or partner, the person who completes a couple.

clue.text: One visiting stops at first by delta in Mississippi maybe

indicators.note: at first points to the beginning, so only the opening letter is used
one piece being in another places it inside that other

blocks.note: the first letter
the Mississippi is an example of a US river
Delta is D in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A tourist calls in, staying first near the delta of the Mississippi.
explanation.walkthrough: The delta of the Mississippi is a real place, which hides that delta is just D. 'Stops' reads as a verb but is the noun, bus stops.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus driver calls at one stop after another along a route, so the definition is a playful description.

clue.text: Wife loathing extremely short, dismissive remark

indicators.note: falling short means stopping before the end, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
hate is loathing
very means extremely

explanation.surface: A wife who can't stand it gives a curt, scornful reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely short' looks like one phrase meaning very brief; it is VERY cut short by a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Said on its own with a shrug, the word is a stock retort showing indifference to what someone has said.

clue.text: Director finished with lists completely

blocks.note: the head of an organisation directs it
something over is finished
a ship that lists heels over to one side

explanation.surface: A manager has fully completed the work on some lists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lists' looks like a noun but is the verb used of a ship leaning over, which also heels.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, best known in being in love that way, means totally and utterly, as when someone falls wholly.

clue.text: A measure of what attracts concertgoers — tedious shows!

indicators.note: to show something is to put it on display, here within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A gauge of what draws people to concerts: dull performances, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What attracts concertgoers' reads as a pop-music question; 'what attracts' is the magnet, and the answer sits across 'concertgoers' and 'tedious'.
explanation.definitionFit: The oersted is the old CGS unit of magnetic field strength, and magnets are things that attract.

clue.text: Gave way after reply, periodically getting jostled

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters
to bow to pressure is to give way

explanation.surface: Someone backed down after answering, now and then being shoved around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' tells you the piece for 'Gave way' comes second, so the alternate letters of 'reply' lead.
explanation.definitionFit: To elbow people is to push them aside with one's arms, the typical crowd shove, so the two verbs match.

clue.text: Hardy perennial, this? Yes and no

definitions.text: Hardy perennial, this? Yes and no

blocks.note: surface reading: a tough evergreen shrub that survives year after year in the garden
setter's reading: the comedian forever partnered with Oliver Hardy, who is part of a perennial double act but is not Hardy himself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Yes and no' is the key: the answer is a hardy perennial plant, yes, but as Hardy's comic partner it is not Hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: The bay tree is a tough evergreen shrub, and Stan of that name partnered Oliver Hardy in a lasting film duo.

clue.text: A sign radio programme has not ended

indicators.note: something that has not reached its end is missing its final letter

blocks.note: A long-running BBC Radio 4 farming soap opera

explanation.surface: A hint that a radio show is still running.
explanation.walkthrough: The Archers, a BBC radio soap since 1951, really has never ended, which is what makes the surface work; cryptically it loses its last S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sagittarius, ninth sign of the zodiac, is depicted as a centaur with a bow, and is called by that English name.

clue.text: Something cracked, holding up energy supply

blocks.note: E is the symbol for energy
a joke is something you crack, and a quip is a joke

explanation.surface: A fault in something broken is disrupting the power supply.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the second piece holds the first up from below, so E sits on top. 'Cracked' suggests damage, but jokes are cracked.
explanation.definitionFit: To equip a team or expedition is to supply it with what it needs, so both are verbs of provisioning.

clue.text: Big, strong guy with paper hanky’s last

indicators.note: the last of a word is its end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: a guy is a man, referred to as he
the FT is the Financial Times newspaper
the final letter

explanation.surface: A large, muscular man with the last of a box of tissues.
explanation.walkthrough: The FT, the Financial Times, is the paper most often clued this way.
explanation.definitionFit: A hefty person is large and powerfully built, so the adjective covers both size and strength at once.

clue.text: Without question a difficulty pulling back loose garment

indicators.note: pulling something back draws it the opposite way, so the letters run backwards
without in its old sense means outside, so one piece stands round the other

blocks.note: a rub is a difficulty, as in 'there's the rub'
Q is the abbreviation for question

explanation.surface: A problem, no doubt about it, retrieving a baggy item of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without question' reads as 'undoubtedly', but 'without' is the old sense outside, wrapped round Q.
explanation.definitionFit: A burqa is a loose outer robe covering a woman's whole body, worn in some Muslim traditions.

clue.text: Parade a symbol of victory that is not shown on BBC

indicators.note: something not shown is kept out of sight, so these letters are taken away

blocks.note: V for victory, the two-finger sign
Auntie is the British nickname for the BBC
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A victory parade with a symbol the BBC declines to broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: The BBC has long been called Auntie, as in 'Auntie Beeb'; it loses IE, so 'that is not shown' does the subtracting.
explanation.definitionFit: To vaunt something is to show it off boastfully, which is the figurative sense of parade as a verb.

clue.text: Decline to show hesitation, becoming vocal patriot?

blocks.note: to flag is to tire or decline in energy
to waver is to hesitate between choices

explanation.surface: Refusing to falter turns someone into a loud nationalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decline' reads as refuse, which leads nowhere; it means to wane, as energy does.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud, demonstrative nationalist is caricatured as waving a national flag, so the compound means an outspoken patriot.

clue.text: Like the clappers are striking: without end?

blocks.note: a rap is a sharp blow or knock
doing something idly is doing it without aim or end in view

explanation.surface: The clappers inside bells keep striking forever, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like the clappers' is British slang for very fast; the bell clappers in the surface really do strike.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from bell clappers swinging furiously, means at great speed, so the adverb is an exact equivalent.

clue.text: Fear led to shift supporting Union

indicators.note: a shift moves things to new positions, so these letters change places

blocks.note: taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: Fear prompted a change of heart in favour of the Union.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital U points to the Union side in the American Civil War, whose troops were called Federals.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Civil War the Federal side backed the Union against the Confederacy, so the adjective means pro-Union.
